title: Rav Huna, son of Rav Natan
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: English translation and editorial notes prepared for Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: He is sometimes called Rav Huna bar Natan.

His father, Rav Natan, was better known through his son and was called “Rav Natan, father of Rav Huna son of Rav Natan,” as explained in his own entry. Rav Huna still had the opportunity to serve Rava and receive teachings from him. In [Nedarim 12a](https://www.sefaria.org/Nedarim.12a),[^1] he explains Rava’s statement, and Rava responds to his words. In [Bava Batra 55a](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Batra.55a), Rav Ashi says: “Huna bar Natan told me: I asked Rava’s scribes,” and so on. He was a principal disciple of Rav Pappa; see [Pesachim 17b](https://www.sefaria.org/Pesachim.17b), [59b](https://www.sefaria.org/Pesachim.59b), [Bava Metzia 66b](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Metzia.66b), Horayot 40b,[^2] [Niddah 43b](https://www.sefaria.org/Niddah.43b), and [Zevachim 41b](https://www.sefaria.org/Zevachim.41b), [91b](https://www.sefaria.org/Zevachim.91b). [Berakhot 42a](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.42a) relates that Rav Pappa visited him. After they had finished their meal, something more to eat was brought before them, and Rav Pappa took some and ate. They questioned him, and he answered: “The statement concerned removing [the table].”[^3] In [Menachot 15a](https://www.sefaria.org/Menachot.15a), he challenges Rav Pappa: “But what of the offerings that ascend [the altar]?” The passage continues: “And furthermore, Rav Ashi said: Come and hear,” and “And furthermore, did not Ravina say …?” These are undoubtedly the anonymous Gemara’s additions, made by those who arranged the Talmud, rather than Rav Huna son of Rav Natan himself challenging Rav Pappa with statements of Rav Ashi and Ravina. The reading should be: “And furthermore, Ravina said.”[^4]

Already in the days of Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, who was then still a young man, Rav Huna was a distinguished scholar.[^5] [Pesachim 86b](https://www.sefaria.org/Pesachim.86b) relates that he once visited Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak’s house. They asked him his name, and he replied, “Rav Huna.” They said, “Let the master sit on the couch,” and he sat down. They offered him a cup; he accepted it at once, drank it in two draughts, and did not turn his face away. They asked him: “Why did you call yourself Rav Huna?” He answered: “That is the name I bear”—that is, “They have called me Rav Huna since childhood.” “Why did you sit down when we told you to sit on the couch?” He replied: “Do whatever the host tells you.” “Why, when we offered you the cup, did you accept it [at once]?” He answered: “One declines an offer from someone of lesser standing, but does not decline one from someone of higher standing,” and so on.

He also received teachings from Ameimar. In [Gittin 19b](https://www.sefaria.org/Gittin.19b), he says, “Thus said Ameimar”; in [Zevachim 19a](https://www.sefaria.org/Zevachim.19a), he says, “When I came before Ameimar”; and in [Kiddushin 72b](https://www.sefaria.org/Kiddushin.72b), Ameimar permitted him to marry a woman from Mechoza.

In Rav Ashi’s time, when Rav Ashi headed the academy at Sura, Rav Huna bar Natan was the exilarch, as Rav Sherira Gaon attests in his [Epistle, part III, chapter 3](https://www.sefaria.org/Epistle_of_Rav_Sherira_Gaon.1.104). Torah learning and high office were thus united in him. Among all the exilarchs mentioned in the Talmud, we find only Rav Huna the exilarch, who died in Rabbi’s lifetime; Mar Ukva, who lived in Shmuel’s time; Rabbana Ukva, Rav’s grandson; and Rav Huna son of Rav Natan, who were also leading Torah scholars of their generations.[^6]

His halakhic teachings occur throughout the Talmud; see [Shabbat 116b](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.116b), [Eruvin 42b](https://www.sefaria.org/Eruvin.42b), [58b](https://www.sefaria.org/Eruvin.58b), [Yoma 87b](https://www.sefaria.org/Yoma.87b), [Bava Metzia 77a](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Metzia.77a), and [Avodah Zarah 24b](https://www.sefaria.org/Avodah_Zarah.24b). We also repeatedly find him with Rav Ashi. In [Gittin 7a](https://www.sefaria.org/Gittin.7a), he asks Rav Ashi, “What is the meaning of the verse …?” Rav Ashi answers, and Rav Huna bar Natan replies: “Do I not know that? Rather, Rav Geviha of Argiza gave an explanation of it.” In [Gittin 19b](https://www.sefaria.org/Gittin.19b), Rav Ashi says: “Huna bar Natan told me: Thus said Ameimar”; and in [Bava Batra 55a](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Batra.55a), “Rav Ashi said: Huna bar Natan told me,” and so on. He also disagrees with Rav Shimi bar Ashi in [Zevachim 30a](https://www.sefaria.org/Zevachim.30a). As for [Ketubot 7a](https://www.sefaria.org/Ketubot.7a), where we find “Rav Nachman said: Huna bar Natan told me,” undoubtedly either this Rav Nachman is Rav Nachman bar Rav Huna, who headed the academy at Sura before Mar bar Rav Ashi, as stated in Rav Sherira Gaon’s [Epistle, part III, chapter 4](https://www.sefaria.org/Epistle_of_Rav_Sherira_Gaon.1.108), or the text should follow the reading of the Rif and the Rosh: “Rav Nachman said: Huna told me.”[^7]

Apart from Rav Ashi, who headed the entire Diaspora, he was the greatest figure of his generation. In [Gittin 59a](https://www.sefaria.org/Gittin.59a), Rav Acha son of Rava says: “From Rabbi’s time until Rav Ashi, we have not found Torah learning and high office united in one person.” The Gemara objects: “Have we not? Was there not Huna bar Natan?” It answers: “Huna bar Natan was different, for he submitted to Rav Ashi.”[^8] Rav Ashi recounts an example of his high standing in [Zevachim 19a](https://www.sefaria.org/Zevachim.19a). Huna bar Natan told him: “Once I was standing before King Izgadar. My belt was too high, and he lowered it for me, saying: ‘It is written of you, “[A kingdom of priests and a holy nation](https://www.sefaria.org/Exodus.19.6).”’ When I came before Ameimar, he said to me: ‘The verse “[Kings shall be your foster-fathers](https://www.sefaria.org/Isaiah.49.23)” has been fulfilled in you.’”

Rav Sherira describes his submission to Rav Ashi in the [Epistle, part III, chapter 3](https://www.sefaria.org/Epistle_of_Rav_Sherira_Gaon.1.103-104): “Throughout all these years after Rav Pappa, Rav Ashi was gaon at Sura … He established for them assemblies and fasts that had previously belonged only to the exilarchs … Huna bar Natan was exilarch in those days, and Meremar bar Zutra—or Meremar and Mar Zutra—who came after him obeyed Rav Ashi and held their assemblies at Mata Mechasya.”[^9]

These words imply that Rav Huna bar Natan died before Rav Ashi. Yet [Moed Katan 28a](https://www.sefaria.org/Moed_Katan.28a)[^10] relates that [the Angel of Death] appeared to Rav Ashi. Rav Ashi asked, “Why such haste?” The answer was: “Bar Natan’s time to take your place is pressing.” [Tosafot on Gittin 59a, beginning “But was there not …?”](https://www.sefaria.org/Tosafot_on_Gittin.59a.9.1) reads: “Huna bar Natan’s time to take your place is pressing.” Their wording implies that Rav Ashi died before Rav Huna bar Natan. Sefer Yuchasin likewise states, in its seventh generation of Amoraim: “After Rav Ashi came Meremar … But it appears to me, from the Talmud at the end of Moed Katan, that Rav Huna bar Natan was head of the academy after Rav Ashi.” Here Sefer Yuchasin is indeed mistaken. What the Gemara means by “Bar Natan’s time to take your place is pressing” is that, after Rav Ashi’s death, Rav Huna bar Natan became the leading figure of the entire generation, and the prestige of the exilarchate returned to its former position: he was no longer subordinate to the head of the academy who succeeded Rav Ashi. It does not mean that Rav Huna bar Natan became head of the academy after him. Rav Sherira is correct that Meremar succeeded Rav Ashi at Sura. The scholar Rabbi Abraham Krochmal, in his *Perushim ve-Ha’arot*, page 60, advances a new suggestion: Meremar, who succeeded Rav Ashi, was Huna bar Natan’s brother, and this is what the Gemara means by “Bar Natan’s time to take your place is pressing.” Rav Sherira’s words lend some support to this, since they suggest that Rav Huna bar Natan died before Rav Ashi. As appears from Rav Sherira’s [Epistle](https://www.sefaria.org/Epistle_of_Rav_Sherira_Gaon.1.110), Mar Zutra succeeded him as exilarch: “In the year 781, on the eighteenth of Tevet, Huna Mari, son of Mar Zutra the nasi, was killed.” It is very plausible that Mar Zutra was Rav Huna bar Natan’s son. His son was named Huna Mari after his paternal grandfather. *Sefer Ha-Keritot*, in its *Yemot Olam* section, reports that Rav Huna the exilarch died in 753. If it means Rav Huna bar Natan, then he lived fifteen years after Rav Ashi.[^11][^12]

notes.text: Hyman gives Nedarim 12b; the exchange with Rava appears on 12a.
The source gives הוריות מ:, “Horayot 40b,” a locator outside the tractate’s folio range. Its intended reference is uncertain.
Rav Pappa distinguishes merely finishing the meal from removing the table, the latter being the endpoint relevant to the ruling discussed there.
Hyman distinguishes the anonymous redactional discussion from Rav Huna’s original challenge. His proposed wording changes “And furthermore, did not Ravina say?” to “And furthermore, Ravina said.”
The compressed relative clause is attached here to its nearest named antecedent, Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak; it does not settle the broader chronology.
“Rabbi” here is Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. “Exilarch” is the head of the Babylonian Jewish community; “high office” translates גדולה in the discussion contrasting political standing and Torah learning.
Hyman offers two alternatives for the apparent chronological difficulty: a later Rav Nachman, or a shorter textual reading without “bar Natan.” He does not settle the identification.
The claims about relative rank and succession, here and below, are Hyman’s historical argument; the differing accounts and his conjectural family relationships are retained.
The source preserves both “Meremar bar Zutra” and “Meremar and Mar Zutra.” The variant changes whether one person or two successors are named.

Hyman gives Moed Katan 22a; the death narrative and the corresponding Tosafot citation are at 28a. The Talmud’s idiom speaks of the successor’s “foot” pressing upon the incumbent, meaning that the successor’s time has arrived.

Hyman presents competing chronological implications rather than a single resolved death date. The dates 781 and 753 are retained without conversion to another calendar; the claimed fifteen-year interval is conditional on his identification of the exilarch.

The Epistle’s editions differ. The Oxford 1888 text reads “Meremar and Mar Zutra” in the first passage, names Rav Yemar as Rav Ashi’s successor, and calls the man executed in 781 “Huna son of Mar Zutra,” without “Mari.” Hyman’s quoted forms and his argument are preserved here. The links use the paragraph numbering of that edition rather than Hyman’s part-and-chapter references.
